scenario.name: AuKill EDR Killer — BYOVD Signed PROCEXP152.SYS PPL Bypass & HVCI Containment
scenario.shortSubtitle: Kernel & BYOVD · Signed Process Explorer Driver, IOCTL 0x8335003C/0004 Kill Loop & CodeIntegrity EID 3077
scenario.overview: Think of a high-security power plant whose sapphire security watchtowers sit behind armored blast doors so even a senior floor manager cannot switch them off. Rather than breaking the doors, an intruder carries in an old factory-stamped brass emergency wrench from an obsolete maintenance kit. Because the wrench still carries an authentic factory stamp, the reactor pit guard waves it straight into the deepest control room. Once plugged into the master power bus, the wrench lets the intruder flip off every watchtower circuit breaker in an endless loop, plunging the plant into darkness right before looting the vaults unless an emerald factory-recall shutter blocks the outdated wrench at the entrance. In this scenario (MITRE T1543.003, AuKill EDR Killer Abusing Signed PROCEXP152.SYS) on SRV-APP-09, ransomware operators abuse a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver chain to blind armored endpoint security sensors from kernel space. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: loading an outdated Microsoft-signed Sysinternals driver into Ring 0, then sending an unauthenticated control code to acquire a kernel handle past PPL protection, then running a continuous terminate loop against EDR services, then contrasting that blinding window against HVCI blocklist enforcement. Steps #1 through #4 trace each driver load, control call, service crash, and block event while the Memory tab contrasts Ring 0 driver dispatch against CodeIntegrity blocklist policy. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event ID 6, System Event ID 7031, and CodeIntegrity Event ID 3077.

stages.title: Signed PROCEXP152.SYS Driver Drop & Kernel Service Load
stages.subtitle: Outdated Microsoft-Signed Sysinternals Driver Passes Standard DSE Into Ring 0
stages.description: Carrying an old brass emergency wrench tucked inside a regular toolkit, the intruder steps up to the heavily guarded reactor pit door. The checkpoint guard inspects only the factory stamp embossed on the handle, confirms it was genuinely forged by the plant builder years ago, and waves the obsolete wrench straight down into the deepest control chamber. With local administrator privileges on SRV-APP-09, aukill.exe (PID 5104, the user-mode BYOVD utility deployed by ransomware affiliates) extracts an embedded copy of PROCEXP152.SYS (an outdated version 16.32 Sysinternals Process Explorer kernel driver carrying a real Microsoft digital signature) into C:\Windows\System32\drivers\ and registers kernel service PROCEXP152. Because Windows Driver Signature Enforcement checks only cryptographic validity by default, the OS loads the vulnerable driver straight into Ring 0 (the highest-privilege kernel layer). Unlike unsigned rootkits that Windows refuses to load, Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD, smuggling a legitimate signed third-party driver that contains dangerous functionality) satisfies standard Authenticode signature checks. Registering the service emits Windows System Event ID 7045 (ServiceType kernel mode driver 0x1) while Sysmon Event ID 6 records the exact driver file path, Microsoft signature string, and SHA-256 hash as the driver maps at kernel base 0xFFFFF80541200000. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ BYOVD DRIVER LOAD / ⇠#1 ACK Signed Valid) from Node ① (#1 AuKill User-Mode Loader) to Node ② (#2 Service Control Manager), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 HVCI Blocklist & SOC SIEM).
stages.mitreTechniqueName: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service (BYOVD)

keySpecs.value: Sysmon Event ID 6 + System Event ID 7045 (Type 0x1)

stages.title: Ring 0 IOCTL 0x8335003C Opens Privileged Handle to PPL EDR
stages.subtitle: Unauthenticated DeviceIoControl Executes ZwOpenProcess From Kernel Mode
stages.description: Down inside the reactor pit, the outdated brass wrench snaps directly onto an unguarded master dial that never asks who is turning it. Because commands coming from the deep reactor pit automatically outrank every upstairs armor plate, the wrench effortlessly clicks open the master lock controlling the sapphire security watchtowers. Modern antivirus and EDR sensors like MsMpEng.exe (PID 2188) run as Protected Process Light (PPL, a Windows security boundary that prevents even local SYSTEM user-mode programs from opening terminate handles to security agents). AuKill sidesteps PPL completely by opening device link \\.\PROCEXP152 (the user-to-kernel communication channel exposed by the loaded driver) and issuing DeviceIoControl code 0x8335003C (a driver command that runs ZwOpenProcess inside kernel Ring 0 without checking whether the caller is genuinely Process Explorer). Inside the driver dispatch handler at 0xFFFFF80541200000, PROCEXP152.SYS executes in kernel mode where EPROCESS.Protection PPL restrictions do not block kernel callers (allowing Ring 0 code to obtain handles to protected processes unconditionally). When aukill.exe passes target PID 2188 in the input buffer, the driver calls kernel ZwOpenProcess (a Ring 0 handle-creation routine that bypasses user-mode access checks) and hands back handle 0x000003A4 carrying full PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS permissions directly into user-mode PID 5104. On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ PPL HANDLE BYPASS / ⇠#2 RET Handle 0x03A4) from Node ② (#2 Service Control Manager) to Node ③ (#3 Ring 0 PROCEXP152.SYS), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 HVCI Blocklist & SOC SIEM).

stages.title: Continuous IOCTL 0x83350004 Loop Blinds All EDR Watchtowers
stages.subtitle: Ring 0 nt!ZwTerminateProcess Defeats SCM Auto-Restart & Silences Heartbeats
stages.description: Holding the unlocked master handle, the intruder cranks the shutoff dial repeatedly in an endless rhythm. One by one, the tall sapphire security watchtowers click dark, and every time an automatic backup generator tries to bring a watchtower back online, the wrench snaps its breaker right back down before a single camera can wake up. Immediately after grabbing handle 0x03A4, aukill.exe invokes DeviceIoControl code 0x83350004 (the driver kill routine that calls nt!ZwTerminateProcess from Ring 0) to terminate MsMpEng.exe and loops continuously across a built-in list of EDR and antivirus process names. Even when the Windows Service Control Manager tries to auto-restart crashed security services, the tight kernel loop kills them again within milliseconds, silencing endpoint telemetry. Because the termination originates from Ring 0 via a Microsoft-signed driver, user-mode self-defense hooks inside the EDR agent never receive an opportunity to block the call. Each forced kill stamps Windows System Event ID 7031 or 7034 (reporting that a critical security service terminated unexpectedly) while the SOC dashboard observes an abrupt drop to zero sensor heartbeats on SRV-APP-09. On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ EDR KILL LOOP / ⇠#3 ACK EID 7031 Burst) from Node ③ (#3 Ring 0 PROCEXP152.SYS) to Node ④ (#4 PPL-Protected EDR Sensors), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 HVCI Blocklist & SOC SIEM).

stages.title: HVCI & Vulnerable Driver Blocklist Catch (CodeIntegrity EID 3077)
stages.subtitle: Stopping Pre-Ransomware Blinding Pre-Load With STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_HASH
stages.description: On an unguarded plant floor, darkness across the watchtowers lets crimson vault-breaking crews rush in unopposed. On the hardened sister plant next door, however, an emerald factory-recall shutter checks the brass wrench serial number at the pit doorway and slams shut instantly, leaving every sapphire watchtower bright and fully armed. Operators deploy AuKill specifically to open a blind window for rapid ransomware staging (such as LockBit or MedusaLocker) with zero active behavioral EDR prevention. Conversely, enabling Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI, which enforces hardware-isolated kernel code checks) alongside Microsoft Recommended Driver Block Rules (a maintained deny-list of known vulnerable signed driver hashes) causes CI.dll to block PROCEXP152.SYS with STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_HASH (0xC0000428) before it ever loads. When CI.dll rejects the revoked driver hash, Windows writes Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational Event ID 3077 naming \Windows\System32\drivers\PROCEXP152.sys and the enforcing block policy (halting the BYOVD chain prior to Ring 0 initialization). Not only does the PPL-protected EDR remain completely intact to quarantine the subsequent ransomware payload, but Event ID 3077 itself serves as a zero-false-positive SOC alarm confirming an active local-admin compromise. On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ HVCI BLOCKED DRIVER / ⇠#4 ACK 0xC0000428) from Node ④ (#4 PPL-Protected EDR Sensors) to Node ⑤ (#5 File Vault & Ransom Stage), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 HVCI Blocklist & SOC SIEM).

steps.diagramAlignment: Follow Step #4 between Node 5 (File Vault & Ransom Stage) and Node 6 (HVCI Blocklist & SOC SIEM) as CI.dll blocks the vulnerable driver pre-load.
steps.detectionAndEvidence: Alert immediately in SIEM via KQL on Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational Event ID 3076 and 3077 referencing PROCEXP152, rtcore64, or truesight, and enforce HVCI + Driver Blocklist via Group Policy or Intune.
